query: FeNiCrCoCu is considered suitable for thin-film use, and its expense favors applying it as a protective coating on conventional metals rather than using it in bulk. Earlier studies examined room-temperature wear behavior in relation to coating–substrate combinations, composition, and grain size, but largely addressed the alloy itself or a limited thermal regime rather than the overall wear response of a coating across different temperatures. Under the constraints that FeNiCrCoCu remains a thin protective coating and that high-temperature wear is the target application, what single testable mechanistic hypothesis could explain what governs its overall wear resistance and why? Specify an intervention relative to a baseline coating condition, predict the observations expected if the hypothesis is correct, state the applicable temperature and loading boundaries, connect the hypothesis to prior evidence, and identify a result that would falsify it.

generation.hypothesis: At high temperatures, the wear resistance of thin-film FeNiCrCoCu coatings is governed by the in situ formation of a continuous, adherent Cr-rich oxide scale. This scale forms via selective oxidation of Cr in the alloy during high-temperature exposure, and it acts as a self-healing protective barrier that reduces friction and abrasive wear under high-load conditions.
generation.material_initial_state: An as-deposited thin-film FeNiCrCoCu coating on a conventional metal substrate with a homogeneous microstructure.
generation.intervention: Apply a controlled pre-oxidation treatment (e.g., hold at ~750°C in air for a set duration) to trigger the selective oxidation of Cr before subjecting the coating to wear testing, compared to an unoxidized baseline coating.
generation.conditions: High-temperature conditions (approximately 700°C–900°C) and high normal loads typical of service conditions where wear resistance is critical.
generation.structural_mediator: A continuous, adherent Cr-rich oxide layer that forms at the surface and along grain boundaries, modifying the local microstructure and serving as a barrier to further oxidation and wear.
generation.mechanism: During high-temperature exposure, Cr in the FeNiCrCoCu coating oxidizes preferentially to form a thin, stable oxide layer. This layer reduces friction by providing a lubricious interface and protects the underlying alloy from direct mechanical damage. Its self-healing nature helps maintain integrity under cyclic high-load sliding, thereby governing the overall wear resistance.
generation.predicted_outcome: If the hypothesis is correct, pre-oxidized coatings will exhibit a significantly lower wear rate and reduced friction during high-temperature sliding tests compared to as-deposited (unoxidized) coatings. Microscopic analysis should reveal an intact, continuous Cr-rich oxide layer on the pre-oxidized samples, while the unoxidized coatings will show more severe wear and less-protective surface oxide characteristics.
generation.baseline: Thin-film FeNiCrCoCu coating in the as-deposited, unoxidized state.
generation.boundary: This mechanism is expected to be effective primarily under high-temperature conditions (700°C–900°C) and under mechanical loads representative of advanced protective applications. Its effectiveness may not translate to low-temperature or very high load-outlier conditions where oxide scale formation or stability might be compromised.
generation.uncertainty: The precise nature, thickness, and long-term stability of the Cr-rich oxide scale in FeNiCrCoCu under cyclic wear conditions require further quantification, and there may be effects from the other elements (e.g., Cu) that could modify the oxidation behavior.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two sets of FeNiCrCoCu thin-film coatings on identical conventional metal substrates. One set receives a controlled pre-oxidation treatment (e.g., exposure to 750°C in air for 1 hour) to promote the formation of the Cr-rich oxide scale, while the other set remains in the as-deposited, unoxidized condition. Both sets are then subjected to identical high-temperature sliding wear tests under a fixed high load at around 750°C.
measurements: Wear volume loss measured by profilometry
Coefficient of friction during the sliding test
Surface oxide scale integrity and composition via SEM/EDS
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the pre-oxidized coatings do not exhibit a statistically significant reduction in wear rate and friction compared to the as-deposited coatings, or if post-test analysis reveals that no continuous, adherent Cr-rich oxide layer has formed (or that it fails to remain intact during wear), then the hypothesis will be considered falsified.

cited_evidence.text: Abstract WVTaTiCr x ( x = 0, 0.25, 0.5, 0.75, 1) refractory high-entropy alloy coatings were prepared on a 42-CrMo steel plate using laser cladding. The purpose of this work is to investigate the effect of the Cr content on the microstructure and properties of the WVTaTiCr x coating. The morphologies and phase compositions of five coatings with different Cr contents were comparatively observed. In addition, the hardness and high-temperature oxidation resistance of the coatings were also analyzed. As a result, with the increase in Cr, the coating grains were more refined. All the coating is mainly composed of the BCC solid-solution phase, which promotes the precipitation of the Laves phase with the increase in Cr. The addition of Cr greatly improves the hardness, high-temperature oxidation resistance and corrosion resistance of the coating. The WVTaTiCr (Cr 1 ) exhibited superior mechanical properties, especially in terms of its exceptional hardness, high-temperature oxidation resistance and outstanding corrosion resistance. High-entropy alloys (HEAs), since their discovery by Yeh et al. in 2004, [1] have opened up researchers to a new alloy system that contains five or more equimolar principal elements. In equimolar HEAs, each element has an equal probability of occupying the lattice sites in a crystal structure such as face-centered cubic (FCC), [2] body-centered cubic (BCC), [3] or hexagonal structure [4] crystal structures. Lattice distortion, sluggish diffusion, high entropy, and cocktail effects have been identified as the core effects contributing to the superior properties, hardness, strength, ductility, erosion, tribocorrosion, corrosion, and oxidation/wear resistance [5] − [7] of HEAs in a wide range of temperatures over conventional alloys. From the viewpoint of applications in extrusion dies and cutting inserts, the cost of metal powders used to develop bulk HEAs can hinder their commercialization as an alternative to the alloys in use.
